events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Omar. As leader I include myself on the opening mission to set the tone, and Omar has given me no cause for concern so far; a small trusted pair keeps Mission 1 simple and gives us a clean read on how the team performs.

I can't support Leo and Omar for Mission 1 as proposed. Leo's reasoning rests on Omar having given no cause for concern so far, but that is a feeling, not evidence. A two-player team that includes the leader gives a small group an easy way to control the mission outcome. I'd rather see a different composition with a clearer basis for trust, so I'm inclined to vote against this team.

Felix, I hear your concern, but let's be honest about what you actually said: you have no evidence either, only a hypothetical. You're worried that a two-player team including the leader is 'an easy way to control the mission outcome' — but that logic applies to literally every opening proposal in a five-player game. Mission 1 requires two people. As leader I must be on the team only if I include myself, and if I pick any two others, we learn even less because I'm the one proposing and I can't be independently evaluated. Including myself is actually the most transparent option: if this mission fails, you can point directly at me and I have nowhere to hide. That's the opposite of 'controlling the outcome' — it's putting my own reputation on the line from turn one. On Omar: 'no cause for concern' is precisely what any player at this table could honestly say on the first mission, including you. There has been no mission, no vote, no behavior to analyze. If we disqualify players for having a clean record, we can never form any team. What matters is what happens next: if Leo and Omar succeeds, both of us build credit; if it fails, Omar and I are the prime suspects and you should remember this moment. I'd ask everyone else to weigh which argument is grounded: my offer of accountability, or Felix's instinct that a normal opening proposal is somehow suspicious. Frankly, Felix, arguing against the standard opening composition with nothing to back it is the kind of noise that only serves to burn through proposals and push us toward rejection chaos. Five rejected teams hands the game to Evil without a single mission being played. I'm keeping the team as Leo and Omar, and I invite the rest of you to judge us by results, not by Felix's vibes.

I'm still voting against Leo and Omar. Leo's answer doubled down on pressure instead of answering the concern. He called my view noise and said we should judge by results, but a bad team can't be judged by results before the mission is played. Choosing himself plus a player with no record gives the leader a team he controls. I'd rather see the mission go to players who haven't been pushed this hard to pass. Omar, you haven't said anything about this team yet. Do you want to be on Mission 1 with Leo, and why do you think Leo's argument about accountability holds up?

Felix, you asked me directly, so I'll answer you plainly: yes, I want to be on Mission 1 with Leo, and yes, I think Leo's accountability argument holds up better than your hypothetical.

On my own reasons: Mission 1 needs two players. Leo proposed himself and me, which means the two people who have behaved most predictably so far are the two on the field. Nobody has said anything about me that isn't a guess about how I'd behave, and I notice the same is true of you — but you treat my silence as suspicious and Leo's as fine, which is inconsistent. If Leo and I fail, the cost lands on exactly the two of us, and that is precisely why I have no incentive to shade this mission: the blame has nowhere to go but to us. That's Leo's whole point, and it survives your objection.

On the substance of your claim: you say a leader who includes himself "controls the outcome" of a two-player team. In a five-player game with a two-person mission, every legal opening team is either leader-plus-one or two others. If we exclude the leader we get a pair we cannot independently evaluate and we learn even less. Leo's choice is the one that puts a name on the failure risk from turn one, and you called that noise. I'd rather be judged by results on the card than by your instinct before a single card is played.

What I actually think is worth worrying about is where this discussion is heading. We've now burned two turns on a proposal that costs nothing, and you've had your say twice without adding a single piece of evidence. Rejected teams pass leadership clockwise, and this table has five players — if we keep rejecting on vibes, the fifth rejection ends the game in Evil's favor before a single mission card is submitted. The Evil team is the only party in this room that benefits from us talking ourselves out of a perfectly ordinary opening pair. I'd like you to ask yourself whether your continued resistance serves them better than it serves us.

I'll also be blunt: if you're prepared to vote against Leo and Omar on no evidence beyond a feeling, then you are the one making a bad decision here, not Leo. So let me put it to you directly — Felix, are you going to approve Leo and Omar, or is your objection going to stand on nothing but tone?

Omar, to answer you directly: no, I'm not approving Leo and Omar. You asked whether my objection rests on tone alone, so here is the substance. Leo's case rests on the fact that nobody has a record yet, but that is true of every opening pair, so it doesn't distinguish this team from a bad one. Leo has now told us twice to judge by results and framed any rejection as the game handing itself to Evil. That pushes us to approve before any information exists, and I'm weighing that pressure as evidence. Omar, you said neither of you has an incentive to shade the mission because the blame lands on the two of you. That is true of any team, so it isn't evidence of anything. I'd like you to answer one specific point: if Mission 1 is a two-player team with no record, what makes this pair more trustworthy than any other pair the leader could pick, and why should the fifth-rejection clock be a reason to approve rather than a reason to propose a different team?

Felix, you asked me two specific things, so I'll answer both directly and then say why I think this table is about to make a mistake.

First: what makes Leo and me more trustworthy than any other pair the leader could pick? Honestly: at Mission 1 there is no record, no card, no behavior to compare. You say that means the argument distinguishes nothing — and you're right that the argument alone distinguishes nothing. But when two options are equally unevidenced, the tiebreaker is not "no evidence," it is who has spent the table's time generating friction for no gain. You have now taken three of the seven turns so far, and what has your opposition produced? A hypothesis about leaders controlling outcomes, and a restatement of the fact that nobody has a history yet. That is your contribution to the discussion.

Second: why should the fifth-rejection clock be a reason to approve rather than a reason to propose a different team? It isn't a reason to approve on its own, and I won't pretend otherwise. But note what it actually is: five rejections on Mission 1 ends the game in Evil's favor with no card ever submitted. That is the only party in this room that wins from continued obstruction — not me, not Leo, but the players whose cards we would never learn to read. If you think Leo and Omar are the wrong pair, name the pair you want instead. You haven't, in three turns. Felix, if you have a better two-player team in mind, put it on the table now, and I will support discussing it seriously. If you don't, then you're asking the table to reject a proposal on the strength of a guess while the countdown to a walkover runs.

And Theo, Amara — you two have been quiet while one player has framed every normal opening proposal as suspicious. Judge the proposal on the only evidence that exists: Leo and I both want this mission to succeed and both bear the full blame if it fails, and nobody has alleged anything specific about either of us. The pair I put my name on is the one where failure is hardest to hide and easiest to assign. Vote for Leo and Omar, and if this mission fails, the two of us are your suspects — that's exactly the accountability Felix said he wanted to see and then refused to accept when it was offered.

I agree with Leo and Omar that Felix's intense opposition is unwarranted. In a five-player game, a leader proposing themselves plus one other player for Mission 1 is standard play. It gives us clear accountability: if the mission fails, we know Evil is between Leo and Omar. Felix spent all three of his speaking turns attacking this proposal without ever suggesting an alternative composition, which feels like manufactured friction rather than helpful deduction. While Omar emphasizing the fifth rejection is a bit premature since this is only the first proposal, approving a clean opening team is generally the right move for Good to get information on the board. Amara, as the only other player who hasn't spoken yet, do you agree with approving Leo and Omar, or do you see any merit in Felix's objections?

Theo, I see some merit in Felix's objection: neither accountability nor the rejection clock makes Leo and Omar more trustworthy than another pair, and the clock is premature on the first proposal. But Felix's argument about leader control also doesn't distinguish this team from other opening pairs. I have no solid reason to reject Leo and Omar, so I'm inclined to approve, while remembering that even a successful mission won't clear either player.

One last word from me, then I'll sit down.

The math here is simple and I'd rather not dress it up. Felix has occupied three turns of this discussion and produced zero concrete allegations about Leo or me — no claim of bad play, no inconsistency in any statement either of us has made, nothing about our cards or our judgment. What he has produced is a general theory that a leader who includes himself on a two-player mission "controls the outcome," which describes every possible opening proposal in a five-player game and therefore rules out nothing. A concern that excludes every alternative is not a concern; it is just opposition.

Compare that with what is actually on the table: Leo and Omar is a two-player team on Mission 1, the smallest team this game will ever ask for. If it succeeds, Good is one card closer to three wins and the table learns something. If it fails, the cost is public and falls on exactly the two of us, and the table learns something even more valuable — that one of us is reading cards wrong. Either outcome, the table gets information. That is the argument for this proposal, and it stands without any appeal to urgency, without the fifth-rejection clock, and without any personal accusation against Felix.

Theo, Amara: you have both said you have no specific reason to reject this team, and Amara, you said so plainly while still crediting Felix's objection as reasonable-sounding — which is a generous read of an argument that never once distinguished this pair from any other pair. I would rather not see good faith extended to a position that has now run out of reasons. The standard opening composition, proposed by the leader who bears the accountability, is what I am asking you to approve. Felix, I am not accusing you of being Evil — I have no basis for that and I won't pretend to one. I am accusing you of spending this table's first proposal on a hypothesis with no evidence behind it, and of asking for a different team without ever naming one. That is the only fault I see in this room, and it is not mine or Leo's.

Vote for Leo and Omar. Let the first card be played so we can start reading the table instead of reading each other.

Leo confirms Leo, Omar. The discussion confirmed the table largely supports this pairing: Theo and Amara both signaled approval, and only Felix objected without ever naming an alternative. Accountability remains maximal — if this mission fails, suspicion lands squarely on me and Omar. I'm keeping the team as Leo and Omar.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Felix proposes Felix, Theo, Amara. As leader for Mission 2, I'm proposing Felix, Theo, and Amara. Mission 1 succeeded with Leo and Omar, and I'm choosing the team with no known Evil players on it, which keeps the mission's outcome in the hands of players I can trust.

Felix, your Mission 2 proposal is Felix, Theo, and Amara, which leaves out Leo and Omar — the two players who actually ran Mission 1, submitted cards, and produced a success with zero fail cards. I want to put the sharpest version of the question I asked you at Mission 1, because it applies to you now: on what evidence, rather than on what instinct, are Leo and Omar excluded?

At Mission 1 you objected that a proposed team needs a distinguishing basis beyond "nobody has been proven evil," and that was fair. But note what has changed since then: Leo and Omar now have the only performance data this table possesses. They succeeded. Theo and Amara have no track record at all — they have never been on a card. Your team therefore puts the two entirely untested players on the field and leaves off the two players who have already faced a card. If Felix, Theo, and Amara succeeds, we learn nothing whatsoever about Leo or Omar, and we go into Mission 3 with the same blank slate we had before Mission 1. If it fails, we finally learn something — about Felix, Theo, and Amara. Either way, the question about the pair that has already been tested gets deferred for free.

There is also a cheap cost to sending this back. We are zero rejections into this mission. A rejected proposal does not hurt the table's chances; it simply passes leadership to the next player clockwise, who gets to put a fresh composition in front of us. The genuinely expensive outcome here is approving a team that excludes two players for reasons nobody in this room has been told.

So for the record, my own position: I would support a team that puts Leo back in the field — Felix, Leo, and one of Theo or Amara. That gives us a tested pair, keeps a leader on the card, and produces information about a player we have never watched read a card.

Felix, I will ask you directly, because you asked me directly at Mission 1 and I owe you the same: what is the evidence you are acting on when you exclude Leo and Omar, and if it is not evidence, why should this table treat your instinct as more reliable than the instincts it declined to act on before Mission 1 was even played?

Omar, you asked what evidence I'm acting on, and I'll answer plainly: I'm not excluding Leo and Omar because of a hidden rule. I'm choosing a team I can explain. Mission 1 succeeding only tells us no Fail cards were played. It does not tell us who chose Success, and a careful Evil player would also produce a zero-fail mission when they want to keep their head down. So the Mission 1 result is not a reason to put the same pair back on the card. It is a reason to test a different pair and see whether the results hold up.

On your point about untested players: Theo and Amara having no record is exactly why this team gives us new information. Mission 2 with Felix, Theo, and Amara shows how two players with no history perform beside me, and Mission 3 then gives us a pattern to compare against. Your argument also leans heavily on the rejection count. Five rejections is a real risk, but a team should be approved because it has a sound basis, not because the table is running out of time. Your pressure on the point about Mission 1 was the same pressure I objected to before, and I don't think it should decide this vote.

Amara, you said earlier that you had no solid reason to reject Leo and Omar, but you also said the rejection clock was premature. Setting aside the clock, do you think a successful Mission 1 with those two is enough reason to repeat the pair, or does a fresh team with a new result give us better information on Mission 2?

Felix, the successful first mission is modest evidence in Leo and Omar's favor, not a clearance. A completely fresh team gives us a different result, but a success still wouldn't clear its members, and a failure would leave three suspects. Since I'm Good, I prefer a team including me, but I don't know whether Felix or Theo is Good. I'd also consider a team including me and someone from the successful pair. For now, I'm inclined to approve Felix, Theo, and Amara, but I don't see a decisive evidential advantage for it.

Felix, you never answered my question. I asked what evidence you were acting on when you excluded Leo and Omar, and what came back was a description of the team you preferred, not evidence against the pair. So let me put the sharper version of the point to the table.

Your Mission 2 team is Felix, Theo, and Amara. Every member of it is untested — not one of you has ever read a card. Leo and Omar are the only players at this table with any performance data at all, and that data is zero fail cards on a two-player mission. Felix, you described that result as not telling us who chose Success, which is fair, but it cuts against you: the same logic applies to you, Theo, and Amara. You have no data on any of yourselves either. On your own reasoning, you are proposing the three least-known players on the board and dismissing the two most-known ones, and then calling it the cautious choice. It is the inverse.

The information problem is worse than that. If Felix, Theo, and Amara succeeds, the table learns nothing about anyone — every player on it is still a blank. If it fails, we get three suspects instead of one or two, which is close to useless. Contrast a team that keeps a tested player on the card alongside new ones: success or failure then tells us something about the tested player too. Keeping one proven element is how you convert a result into actual information instead of noise. This is the same argument you found so persuasive at Mission 1, when I told you the fifth-rejection clock was a reason to discuss a different team rather than to approve on instinct — and the same answer is still owed to me.

There is one more consideration that nobody has mentioned, and it should worry all of you. Good wins after three successful missions, and then Evil gets exactly one guess at Merlin among four people. Every Good success we concede shortens the amount of time we have to learn who is who, and shrinks the field the assassin has to work with. The value of a failure here is not the failure itself — it is that it returns time and evidence to the table. Approving an all-untested team because it feels safe is how you donate both.

So my position, stated plainly: I want a team with Leo and Omar on it plus one of you — Felix, Leo, and Omar, or Leo, Omar, and Theo — so the table gets a control alongside the new information. Felix, you say you are choosing a team you can explain, so explain this: on what basis, other than that you prefer it, does a team of three players with no record outrank one that includes the only two players who have ever passed a mission cleanly?

Omar, I'll answer your question directly. My basis is not taste. Mission 1 succeeding with zero Fail cards tells us the team did not sabotage, but it does not tell us whether the two players chose Success because they were Good or because they were keeping their heads down. Any Evil player on that team would produce the same result, so repeating the pair mostly repeats the same ambiguity. A fresh team gives an independent result, which is information we would not get by reusing the first pair. You say my team has no record and is therefore a blank slate. That is true, but the Mission 1 pair also had no record before it was played, and the table approved it on the same kind of trust you now ask me to extend. I am not asking anyone to accept this team on instinct. I am pointing out that this team has no known Evil players on it, and that cannot be said for the pair you keep returning to. You also keep saying that rejecting this team hands the game to Evil. We are zero rejections deep, and one rejection costs nothing. Your repeated focus on the fifth-rejection clock and on the same pairing is pressure, and pressure is not evidence. I would ask the table to judge the Mission 2 team on its composition and on the test it gives us. Theo, you have not yet given your view on this Mission 2 team. Do you think a fresh three-player team gives better information than repeating the pair that already passed a mission, and what would you change about it?

Felix, to answer your question directly: I don't think we should treat Leo and Omar as completely cleared. It's standard for an Evil player on a two-person Mission 1 to play Success to build trust, so your skepticism that at least one of them could be Evil is mathematically sound and consistent with your vote against them on Mission 1. However, completely excluding both of them carries a major risk: if Leo and Omar happen to both be Good, then the two Evil players would have to be you and Amara, meaning your proposed team would contain two Evil players alongside me.

That said, I find Omar's reaction to your proposal concerning. In his last speech, Omar argued that 'the value of a failure here is not the failure itself — it is that it returns time and evidence to the table.' Good never benefits from a failed mission; Evil only needs three fails to win outright, so treating a failure as useful information to prolong the game is dangerous logic.

A balanced team composition might carry forward one player from Mission 1 rather than either freezing both out or taking both blindly. Before deciding how to vote on Felix, Theo, and Amara, I want to hear from Leo, who led Mission 1 and hasn't spoken yet on this proposal. Leo, what is your assessment of Felix completely cutting you and Omar from Mission 2, and what team composition do you think gives us the safest path forward?

Theo, you asked me directly, so here is my assessment. Being cut from Mission 2 alongside Omar, with zero allegations against either of us and a clean Mission 1 result on the board, is not caution — it is Felix repeating the same move he made at Mission 1, just in the other direction. Before Mission 1, he objected to the standard opening pair with no evidence. Now he is excluding the only two players with any performance data, again with no evidence. He says a careful Evil player would play Success on a two-person mission to keep their head down. Fine — but that logic applies to every player at this table, including the three he just put on the team. You cannot selectively apply 'success proves nothing' to Leo and Omar while treating Felix, Theo, and Amara's total blank slate as a virtue. On his own reasoning, he has proposed the three least-known players in the game and called it the trustworthy option. Let me also state plainly what I think the safest composition is, since Theo asked. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards. That is modest evidence, not clearance — I agree with Amara and Theo on that. But the answer to 'modest evidence' is not to throw both tested players off the board. It is to build a team that carries the tested pair forward alongside a new player, so the next result actually tells us something about someone. My proposal: Leo, Omar, and one of Felix, Theo, or Amara. If it succeeds, the new player builds credit next to a proven pair. If it fails, suspicion lands on exactly three named people, and the new player is the most likely suspect given our record. That is a real experiment. Felix's team, by contrast, produces a result we cannot attribute to anyone — three blanks, success teaches nothing, failure hands us three suspects at once. One more thing on Theo's point about Omar's language. I don't read Omar as saying Good benefits from failure — no Good player should ever want a failed mission, and I don't. His point, as I understand it, was that an information-free approval is the worst of both worlds, and on that he is right. A mission that teaches us nothing about anyone is a wasted round, and Good does not have rounds to waste when every success shrinks the field before the endgame. So my position is simple: I will vote against Felix, Theo, and Amara, because it excludes two players for no stated reason and guarantees an unattributable result. I will vote for any three-person team that includes both me and Omar plus one other, and I'd accept a team with me plus two of you as a second-best option. Felix, since you keep saying your choices are about explainable reasoning rather than instinct: explain to the table what specifically about my Mission 1 performance justifies removing me, when the only fact we have about me is that

Omar and Leo keep arguing that the Mission 1 success means their pair should stay on the card, but a success with zero fail cards only tells us the two of them did not sabotage. Their recent speeches lean on pressure about the rejection clock and on who has no record yet, rather than on any specific reason this three-player team is unsafe. I'm voting to approve Felix, Theo, and Amara. I'm not asking anyone to trust me on instinct. This team gives us a fresh, independent result, and no one on it has done anything that raises a specific concern. Omar's claim that a failure is useful because it returns time to the table is the kind of reasoning Good should be wary of, since Good never benefits from a failed mission. Leo's answer to Theo repeated the same pressure, which is not evidence. Theo, you asked for a balanced composition, and I agree we should keep the team small and clean. If anyone can name a concrete action from this game that makes Omar or Leo safer than the three of us, I'd like to hear it now. Otherwise I'd ask the table to approve the team as proposed and let the mission show us more.

Felix has now made four separate arguments and I want to name what they have in common: none of them is about Felix, Theo, and Amara being safer, and all of them are about Leo and Omar being riskier. Let me sharpen that asymmetry, because Felix's own stated standard destroys it.

Felix's case for excluding the tested pair is that a zero-fail success proves nothing, since a careful Evil player would also play Success to keep their head down. Fine. But Felix applies that standard only downward. Apply it to his own team and it is devastating: Felix, Theo, and Amara have no record at all, which means there is nothing about any of them that has been checked, ever, and nothing about them that ever could be. Leo and Omar have an outcome on the board. Under Felix's own logic, "success proves nothing" means untested players are the least verifiable players in the game, not the most. Felix has proposed the three players whose trustworthiness he cannot even point to a single fact about, and called that caution.

There is also the structural point Felix keeps skipping. Good needs three successes to win. If we approve Felix's team and it succeeds — and on Felix's own reasoning it is a team of three blanks, so it is a coin flip dressed up as information — we are one success from ending the game having identified nobody, and then Evil gets one guess at Merlin among four players, blind. Felix's team doesn't just teach us nothing on the result; it teaches us nothing for the endgame either, because every remaining mission will be chosen under the same information vacuum. Felix is proposing the route that lets the game end without the table ever learning a single name. A team that carries one tested player onto the card converts a result into evidence, whichever way the cards fall.

And let me correct the framing Felix keeps attacking, because Theo raised it and it deserves a fairer statement than Felix gives it: Good does not want failure, and I don't want failure. But Good has three successes available and Evil has only two lives before an outright win, while Evil also gets a free shot at Merlin if Good reaches three successes blind. One mission's worth of information is worth one of Evil's three fail cards. Felix's version trades the only thing this table has — the ability to read cards as they come — for a preference he has never grounded.

Amara, you said last turn that you'd also consider a team including you alongside someone from the successful pair. Felix's team includes you and excludes both of them. Which is it, and does a success by three players with no record under Felix's own logic really clear any of you, or does it simply leave us where we started with one fewer mission?

Omar, those positions are consistent: I prefer a team with me and would consider either this proposal or one including a Mission 1 player. A success by Felix, Theo, and Amara would be useful, but it would not clear anyone. The same is true of repeating Leo and Omar.

I disagree that a failed mission is worth trading for information. Successes bring Good closer to winning, and the Assassin's guess remains uncertain even if we haven't identified Evil. Your argument understates that cost.

I still lean toward approving Felix, Theo, and Amara because I know I am Good, though I cannot verify the other two. The first mission's success is modest evidence for Leo and Omar, not proof that they are a safe pair.

Felix has now answered the table four times, and every answer has the same shape: he never says why his team is safe, only why Leo and Omar are unproven. Let me hold him to the standard he keeps claiming to use. At Mission 1 he told us a proposal needs a distinguishing basis, not just a feeling. By that standard his own Mission 2 team fails his own test twice over. First: Felix, Theo, and Amara are the three players with the least information on the board, not the most. Under Felix's own doctrine that 'a careful Evil player would play Success to keep their head down,' a clean record is worthless as clearance — and having no record at all is even weaker. Felix has applied his skepticism in exactly one direction, always away from his own team and always at the two players who are the only ones with any result on the table. That asymmetry is the tell. A player genuinely searching for Evil applies the same bar to everyone; a player managing a narrative applies it selectively. Second: think about what this proposal does to the game's information economy. Three untested players submit cards. If it succeeds, nothing is learned about anyone — Felix said so himself when he dismissed our Mission 1 result. If it fails, we get three suspects at once with no way to separate them. Felix's team is engineered, whether by intent or by carelessness, to produce results that cannot be attributed. Compare a team that keeps a tested player on the card: every outcome then lands on a known baseline. That is the composition I argued for and I still stand behind it — Leo, Omar, plus one of the three, or failing that, me plus two of you. Third, and I want the table to weigh this carefully: look at the pattern across both of Felix's proposals. At Mission 1 he opposed the standard opening pair. Now, as leader, he excludes that exact pair — the only players with a demonstrated clean result — while describing his own untested trio as 'players I can trust.' Trust based on what? He has never named one fact about Theo or Amara that makes them safer than Omar or me. He was given the question directly, twice, and both times he answered with a restatement of his preference. On the first mission I offered the table full accountability: if our mission had failed, suspicion had nowhere to go but to us. It did not fail. Felix responded by pushing the tested players off the board entirely. I will say it plainly: a leader who cuts the only proven pair with no stated reason, while pressuring the table to approve an all-blank team, is not exercising caution — and if this mission goes sideways, the top of my suspect list is already written. Theo, you raised the sharpest point of this discussion yourself: if Leo and Omar are both Good, then two of

I'll finish the thought my last turn was cut off on, because it matters. Theo's own logic cuts directly against Felix's team. If Leo and Omar are both Good — and our Mission 1 result is the only evidence on the board — then both Evil players sit inside Felix, Theo, and Amara, and Felix has proposed a team that could contain both of them at once. Approving that trio blind means that if this mission fails, the table faces a three-person pool with no baseline to separate anyone. If it succeeds, we learn nothing about anyone, exactly as Felix himself argued when he dismissed our result. Either branch of the tree leaves Good poorer.

Felix's answer, for the fourth time now, is the same shape: success proves nothing about Leo and Omar, pressure is not evidence, approve my team. Notice what he still has not done after four opportunities: he has not named one fact about Theo or Amara that makes them safer than Omar or me. Not one. His entire case is that our evidence is inconclusive — but inconclusive evidence still outranks no evidence, and Felix is the one asking the table to swap a known baseline for a blank slate. At Mission 1 he demanded a distinguishing basis for a proposal; his own proposal cannot pass his own test.

The composition that actually serves Good is the one I named last turn: Leo, Omar, plus one of the three. It carries the tested pair forward, puts a new player under observation beside them, and every possible result attributes cleanly. If it succeeds, the new player builds credit next to a proven pair. If it fails, the new player is the prime suspect, because Omar and I would have to have failed it together — which, if you believe our Mission 1 record, you shouldn't.

Amara, you said yourself last turn that you would consider a team including you alongside someone from the successful pair, and that a success by Felix, Theo, and Amara would not clear anyone. I'm asking you directly: would you support Leo, Omar, and Amara for Mission 2? It matches your stated preference exactly — you're on the card, one tested player rides alongside you, and the result tells the table something about you either way. If you'd approve that composition, say so now, because Felix's team is the only alternative on the table and it excludes the only players with a record while including three with none.

To everyone: Felix is asking you to approve the least attributable team this game can produce, proposed by the same player who spent Mission 1 objecting to the most attributable one. That asymmetry is not caution. If this mission goes sideways under Felix's composition, remember who built it and who pushed for it.

Leo, yes, I would consider approving Leo, Omar, and Amara, but I haven't decided it is safer than Felix's proposal. The first mission's success is modest evidence in your favor, not proof that either of you is Good.

Your claim that a failure on Leo, Omar, and Amara would make me the prime suspect overstates that evidence. Either you or Omar could have played Success on Mission 1 and Fail on Mission 2; one Fail is enough. Nor does a successful mission by Felix, Theo, and Amara teach us nothing—it would be modest evidence for that team, just as Mission 1 was for yours.

I still lean toward approving Felix's proposal because it includes me, though I cannot verify Felix or Theo.

Amara rightly dismantled Leo's logic: if a team of Leo, Omar, and a third player were to fail, the third player would not be the automatic prime suspect. It is standard for Evil to play Success on a two-person Mission 1 to build trust, so a Fail on Mission 2 could just as easily come from Leo or Omar. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
